title: Is Occupational Safety a Growing Career?
description: Explore occupational safety career growth, daily work, pay, training and credentials so you can decide whether this field fits your goals.
author: Career Education Institute Curriculum Team
coverAlt: Occupational safety specialist coaching a worker during a factory safety walk-through
body:
Is occupational safety a growing career? Yes. The labor data used on this site projects 18.5% employment growth for occupational health and safety specialists from 2025 to 2035, much faster than the overall job market. The field also has about 17,100 annual openings. That outlook is encouraging, but growth alone does not make a career a good fit. You also need to like field inspections, documentation, training, regulations and speaking up when work is unsafe.

## Why is occupational safety growing?

Occupational safety specialists help employers prevent injuries and illnesses before they happen. They inspect workplaces, identify hazards, develop safety programs, train employees, investigate incidents and track corrective actions. Their work can support construction, manufacturing, energy, healthcare, logistics and government settings.

The need is broad because hazards change with the workplace. A construction site may need help with fall protection, excavations and equipment. A warehouse may focus on forklifts, traffic paths and material handling. A plant may need controls for machinery, chemicals, noise and energy isolation. A specialist has to understand the work well enough to recommend controls that people can actually use.

The projected growth rate reflects the occupation as a whole, not a promise about one employer or city. Employers may hire safety professionals as operations expand, regulations change, facilities add equipment or leadership wants a stronger prevention program. Openings can also come from people leaving the occupation or moving into management.

## What does an occupational safety specialist do?

The work combines time in the field with office and computer work. A normal day might include a toolbox talk, a site walk, a job hazard analysis, an incident interview, a training session and a report for management. Some roles stay in one facility, while others travel between sites.

Common responsibilities include:

- Inspecting work areas, equipment and procedures for hazards
- Breaking jobs into steps and identifying ways to control each hazard
- Writing or updating safety programs and procedures
- Training employees on safe work practices and regulatory topics
- Investigating incidents and near-misses to find contributing causes
- Maintaining injury and illness records and tracking corrective actions
- Working with supervisors, employees, insurers, regulators and management

This is not only a desk job and it is not only enforcement. Strong specialists learn how work is really done, listen to the people doing it and help improve the system. They may need to stop or change a task when there is an immediate danger, but they also spend time coaching, explaining and following up.

> A useful test is to spend time observing a safety professional or coordinator if you can. Notice how much of the job involves people, writing and follow-through in addition to hazard recognition.

## What is the pay and job outlook?

The site’s labor data lists a median annual wage of **$90,150** for occupational health and safety specialists. The middle half of reported wages runs from **$69,560** at the 25th percentile to **$111,690** at the 75th percentile. The 10th percentile is **$55,000**, and the 90th percentile is **$134,950**. These figures are BLS, May 2025. They describe the occupation across the United States, not a guaranteed starting wage or a specific offer.

Employment is projected to grow **18.5% from 2025 to 2035**, with about **17,100 annual openings**. The data lists employment of **143,100**. Your opportunity can still vary by location, industry, education, prior experience, travel requirements and the size of the employer.

The numbers are most useful when you compare them with the work itself. A strong outlook does not remove the need to learn regulations, write clearly, investigate carefully and earn trust with workers and supervisors. Use the [occupational safety specialist salary page](/careers/occupational-safety-specialist/salary/) for the wage figures, then read the [occupational safety specialist career profile](/careers/occupational-safety-specialist/) to connect the data with daily responsibilities.

## How do you enter the field?

A bachelor’s degree in occupational safety, environmental health, industrial hygiene or a related subject is typical for the specialist role. The career profile also notes that some people enter from the trades with an associate degree or extensive safety training and experience. That means there is more than one starting point, but employers can set different requirements for different jobs.

Training usually takes time because you need both technical knowledge and experience with real work environments. The site lists a broad preparation range of two to four years. A practical sequence may look like this:

1. Build science, math, writing and technical-reading skills.
2. Study occupational safety, environmental health or a related field, or build a trade foundation with safety responsibilities.
3. Complete relevant safety training, such as OSHA 30 or topic-specific courses, when it fits the role.
4. Gain experience through a safety coordinator, technician, trade or operations position.
5. Add credentials that match your work, experience and career direction.

The [how to become an occupational safety specialist guide](/careers/occupational-safety-specialist/how-to-become/) explains the path in more detail. Career Education Institute training can help you review foundational concepts and vocabulary, but it does not replace an employer’s requirements, supervised experience, a degree or a professional credential.

## Which credentials can help?

Credentials are not interchangeable, and no single certificate guarantees a job. The right choice depends on the work you already do and the direction you want to take.

The career profile lists several examples:

- **ASP and CSP:** Board of Certified Safety Professionals credentials for broader safety practice and advancement.
- **CHST and OHST:** Credentials for construction health and safety or occupational health and safety technology.
- **OSHA 30 and trainer courses:** Training that can support workplace safety knowledge and, for some roles, employee instruction.
- **CIH:** A credential for specialists whose work centers on industrial hygiene and exposure hazards.

Before paying for a credential, read job postings in the industry you want to enter. Compare the experience, education and exam requirements. Ask an employer which credentials are useful at the coordinator, specialist and manager levels. You can also use the site’s [occupational safety specialist training page](/training/occupational-safety-specialist/) to review a structured learning option.

## What skills matter most?

Hazard recognition is important, but it is only part of the job. You also need to explain risk in plain language, write useful procedures and follow corrective actions until they are complete. A specialist who finds problems but cannot build cooperation will have difficulty creating lasting change.

The strongest skills include:

- Careful observation during inspections and job reviews
- Persuasive communication and respectful coaching
- Clear writing for procedures, reports and training materials
- Calm, fair incident investigation
- Comfort with regulations, records and measurable follow-up
- Willingness to work both indoors and outdoors

The work can be meaningful because your decisions may prevent someone from being injured. It can also be stressful after a serious incident or when a supervisor resists a needed change. The [workplace safety basics guide](/guides/workplace-safety-basics/) is a useful place to review the prevention mindset behind the role.

## Is occupational safety a good fit for you?

Ask yourself how you respond to responsibility and disagreement. You may enjoy this career if you want to protect people, like teaching, can speak up respectfully and enjoy moving between field conditions and organized documentation. You may struggle if you strongly dislike regulations, writing, travel, changing conditions or conversations about unsafe behavior.

You should also think about the setting. Safety specialists may work around construction, machinery, chemicals, vehicles, noise or weather. They wear the same protective equipment required in the areas they inspect and must model the behavior they expect from others.

Before enrolling, collect evidence about your fit:

- Read several local safety coordinator and specialist job postings.
- Compare the education and experience requirements that repeat.
- Ask a current safety professional what takes most of their time.
- Visit a workplace or training session if you have access to one.
- Write down the travel, schedule and field conditions you can accept.

This process can show whether you are drawn to prevention work itself or only to the growth statistic. Both pay and outlook matter, but the daily work decides whether you will stay and develop.

## Next steps

Occupational safety is a growing career by the site’s labor data, with 18.5% projected growth from 2025 to 2035 and about 17,100 annual openings. The best fit is someone who wants to combine hazard recognition, teaching, documentation and practical problem-solving across real workplaces.

Start with the [occupational safety specialist profile](/careers/occupational-safety-specialist/), compare the [training option](/training/occupational-safety-specialist/), and review the [Career Match Quiz](/quizzes/career-match/) if you are considering several paths. Then contact a local employer or safety professional with specific questions about education, field experience, credentials and the kind of work you would do during your first year.
